detail.abstract: The global COVID-19 pandemic acted as a profound catalyst, forcing an unprecedented and rapid shift to remote learning and exposing both the potential and the deep-seated vulnerabilities within global education systems. This paper argues that the post-pandemic educational landscape is irrevocably shifting towards a hybrid learning model, which integrates face-to-face instruction with technology-mediated learning experiences. This transition is not merely a temporary adjustment but a fundamental restructuring of pedagogical delivery, with Educational Technology (EdTech) at its core. The paper explores the dual role of EdTech as both an enabler of flexibility, personalization, and accessibility, and a potential amplifier of existing inequalities the "digital divide." Through a thematic analysis of recent literature, this study examines key themes, including the redefinition of teacher and student roles, the importance of digital pedagogy over mere tool usage, and the critical need for robust infrastructure and educator professional development. The conclusion posits that the successful implementation of a hybrid future is contingent upon a strategic, equitable, and pedagogically grounded integration of EdTech, moving beyond emergency remote teaching to create a more resilient, inclusive, and effective educational ecosystem.

title: Rough Volatility and Slow-Fast Dynamics: Empirical Evidence from VIX and Theoretical Connections
affiliations: University of Bari

detail.title: Rough Volatility and Slow-Fast Dynamics: Empirical Evidence from VIX and Theoretical Connections
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the roughness of financial volatility using daily VIX data from 1990-2024 and a unified pipeline of scaling, entropy, and nonlinear diagnostics. We confirm the stylized fact that volatility is rough, with Hurst exponent H ≈ 0.1, and identify a robust scale break around 45 days. Beyond exogenous fractional models, entropy and surrogate analyses reveal deterministic slow-fast structure consistent with Rulkov-type dynamics. These findings suggest that rough volatility and slow-fast coupling are complementary paradigms: the former captures statistical scaling laws, while the latter offers a potential microstructural mechanism. Incorporating both perspectives improves the forecasting of tail-risk events and strengthens the theoretical link between physics-inspired dynamical systems and financial market modeling.

title: Robust Persuasion under Costly Attention

detail.title: Robust Persuasion under Costly Attention
detail.abstract: We study how Sender should persuade Receiver whose attention technology is unknown, and characterize the worst-case (robust) payoff for Sender. Receiver's attention is costly. Sender, however, does not exactly know the attention costs and what information Receiver pays attention to. Both players know the basic attention technology that is always available to Receiver, which means Receiver can actually have better attention technologies than the basic one for Receiver's objective. However, some better attention technology for Receiver can be worse for Sender's objective at the same time. Thus, Sender chooses an optimal information policy, assuming Receiver's attention technology would be the worst for Sender between attention technologies better than the basic one. Sender's robust payoff is obtained from the information policy that minimizes Sender's payoff over the set of information policies that guarantee Receiver's basic-optimal payoff. Sender has an incentive to disclose information that is more favorable to Receiver if the basic attention technology becomes coarser. We apply our results to (1) Human Resources Team and Junior, where Sender's and Receiver's preferences are aligned, and (2) Seller and Buyer. Under aligned preferences, Sender always commits to the fully informative policy and grants Receiver full discretion in processing information. In Seller-Buyer case, upper censorship is an optimal information policy for Sender, which implies that the classic result in literature robustly holds.

title: Populism, Technocracy, and Party Democracy in Immigration Rhetoric: Testing Caramani's Triangular Framework (2018-2020)

detail.title: Populism, Technocracy, and Party Democracy in Immigration Rhetoric: Testing Caramani's Triangular Framework (2018-2020)
detail.abstract: Contemporary representative democracies are increasingly characterized by what Caramani (2017) identifies as a "triangular relationship" between party democracy, populism, and technocracy. While extensive research has mapped the attitudinal profiles of citizens who align with these three forms of representation, significantly less attention has been paid to how political actors themselves articulate these competing visions in their public discourse. This study addresses this gap through a systematic qualitative content analysis of political rhetoric on immigration-a highly salient issue-during the critical period of 2018-2020. We examine the discourse of three distinct actor types: a populist leader (Matteo Salvini), technocratic institutions (European Central Bank), and party-democratic leaders (Emmanuel Macron and Democratic Party leaders). Our analysis reveals distinct rhetorical patterns that align closely with Caramani's theoretical predictions. Populist discourse employs moralistic, anti-elite language with clear us-versus-them framings; technocratic discourse utilizes depoliticized, data-driven economic analysis; while party-democratic discourse emphasizes pluralism, compromise, and institutional solutions. These findings provide crucial empirical validation of Caramani's framework while demonstrating how abstract theoretical principles manifest in concrete political communication strategies. The study contributes to our understanding of democratic representation by bridging theoretical work on representation with empirical analysis of elite political discourse. **This paper is a work in progress. Comments and feedback are warmly welcomed.

detail.abstract: This paper develops Institutional Capacity Gradient Theory (ICGT) as an operational framework for designing development interventions in fragile states. Rather than claiming to predict which interventions succeed, ICGT provides diagnostic tools and design principles for calibrating interventions to institutional absorption capacity. Building on New Structural Economics (Lin, 2012) and political economy of state-building (Bueno de Mesquita et al., 2003), the framework conceptualizes institutional capacity as a multidimensional vector (C T , C P , C E) representing technical, political, and epistemic capacity. ICGT's contribution is operational: it specifies how to diagnose capacity constraints, match intervention requirements to capacity levels, design performance-based transfer mechanisms, and identify ex ante when interventions will face political economy barriers. The framework makes capacity building legible as an engineering problem with known failure modes, rather than treating it as an art dependent on tacit knowledge. Three case studies-Rwanda, Ethiopia, Afghanistan-illustrate the diagnostic logic and design principles. The paper concludes by specifying what rigorous testing would require, acknowledging current empirical limitations.

publicationDetails.detailsText: ENEECO-D-25-02969

detail.abstract: Using a quantitative, life-cycle model calibrated to U.K. data we examine homeowners’ decisions regarding green technology adoption (heat pumps). Given the empirical residential and wealth distributions, the model is consistent with historically low adoption rates. Counterfactuals show that fiscal policy can increase uptake. Subsidies to installation costs provide immediate incentives to adopt for less wealthy households due to liquidity constraints. Lower electricity taxes incentivize adoption among wealthier households and shift the fiscal liability to the future. Commodity price uncertainty affects adoption rates more when changing electricity taxation but does not change the (unintended) distributional differences across policies.

title: Myopia, Heterogeneity, and Stability
affiliations: Università di Roma "Tor Vergata" and Roma Tre University

detail.title: Myopia, Heterogeneity, and Stability

publicationDetails.detailsText: ECMODE-D-25-02892

detail.abstract: This paper examines how an economy characterized by heterogeneous entrepreneurs, borrowing constraints, and myopic agents responds over time to a transitory shock that ultimately affects aggregate TFP. We introduce a characterization of myopia in which agents systematically extrapolate current conditions into the future, so that long-run forecasts remain anchored to the present and adjust only gradually over time. We consider two types of shocks: one to the parameter measuring inequality and another to the parameter reflecting credit market conditions. In both cases, along the transition path—and in contrast to the perfect-foresight benchmark—myopia: (i) significantly amplifies consumption volatility among workers, and (ii) dampens aggregate output fluctuations. Moreover, we show that under myopic expectations, sufficiently large temporary inequality shocks can induce dynamic instability in the economy.

title: Bargaining on Behalf of Others and How to Fix It for Political Gridlocks and Labor Strikes

detail.title: Bargaining on Behalf of Others and How to Fix It for Political Gridlocks and Labor Strikes
detail.abstract: This paper models bargaining where each side has a principal and replaceable agents. Such bargaining occurs when congressional representatives are bargaining for legislation on behalf of voters or when a firm and a union are bargaining for a labor contract. If agents who bargain have incomplete information and are unsure about what offers will be accepted, their principal may replace agents who do not bargain aggressively, thinking that the agents may have high bargaining costs. To avoid replacement, agents may act excessively aggressively to signal that they have lower bargaining costs, even if they believe that aggression is harmful to their principal. The social cost of bargaining can be lowered by forcing agents to bargain in arduous conditions or by taxing both sides for bargaining time. This tax can replace labor strikes.

detail.abstract: This is not just another economics course. This is the beginning of a new way of seeing the world. For centuries, we have been told that economics is inherently messy, a subjective dance of ideology and intuition. We've accepted that boom-and-bust cycles are inevitable, that persistent unemployment is a fact of life, and that economists will forever disagree on the most fundamental questions. What if everything we've been told is wrong? What if economics could be as reliable, as predictive, and as powerful as physics? This first lecture is your entry point into that reality. title: Attribute associations of municipal green bond yield spreads: A demand perspective

detail.title: Attribute associations of municipal green bond yield spreads: A demand perspective

publicationDetails.detailsText: ENEECO-D-25-03085

detail.abstract: Investor demand and bond structuring attributes jointly shape the pricing of green municipal bonds. We introduce a yield-to-maturity–based approach to measuring municipal green bond spreads and apply it to the California market between 2016 and 2024. These spreads are on average positive but turned negative after 2022. Using Association Rule Learning, we identify that positive spreads are associated with taxable, at-par, callable, and long-maturity bonds, whereas negative spreads are linked to more complex combinations including low spreads at issuance, non-callable, tax-exempt, at-premium, and short-maturity bonds. We further demonstrate that international demand matters: stronger bidding in Japanese Treasury auctions systematically raises issuance yields for U.S. municipal green bonds, particularly in higher-order attribute groups. These results show how structuring attributes and cross-border demand jointly shape green bond pricing, offering practical insights for issuers seeking to optimize financing costs and for investors navigating sustainability-driven markets.

detail.title: What Drives Capital to Green Companies in Emerging Markets: Evidence from Investment Funds

publicationDetails.detailsText: ENEECO-D-25-03167

detail.abstract: Leveraging on a security-level dataset of the 37 000 largest investment funds globally, this paper provides the first mapping of investment funds’ holdings in “green” companies (classified specifically at the security level as companies with revenues in renewable energy, green transport and buildings) in Emerging Markets (EMs). This overcomes reliance on typical ESG measures suffering from greenwashing. Despite a boom in “sustainable” investing, investments in EM green companies remain minuscule and heavily skewed towards China. Fund-level regressions demonstrate that younger, retail and domestic funds are significantly more likely to invest in green companies, as they may be better able to overcome information asymmetries. In contrast, global funds invest in green in countries with both stronger “investibility” and “greenness” criteria: with higher benchmark weights, higher portfolio flows openness, renewable exports and energy generation and mandatory environmental disclosure. These results have important policy implications regarding the role that capital markets can play in the low-carbon transition: index inclusion, maintaining open capital account, and developing strong green sectors can position countries as prime destinations for green finance.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the impact of a significant minimum wage increase in Türkiye on infant birth weight and neonatal health. We utilize data from the Türkiye Demographic and Health Survey to investigate the birth outcomes of babies exposed to a 30% minimum wage hike during pregnancy. Leveraging variation in the predicted probability that a household includes a minimum-wage earner, we estimate a difference-indifferences model to identify the causal effect of prenatal exposure to the minimum wage increase. Our analysis reveals that exposure to a higher minimum wage during pregnancy significantly increases birth weight and reduces the likelihood of low birth weight (< 2500 grams). We find no difference in the gestational length or the possibility of receiving prenatal health care, employment status, or smoking behavior for mothers who face an increase in the minimum wage while pregnant. detail.abstract:
Europe’s live-in caresector faces a triple challenge: growing demand for elderly care all over Europe, care drain towards western countries, and the widespread informality of live-in caregiving work. Undeclared employment remains widespread , –estimates indicate about 6.8 million undeclared workers in personal and household services sector (home based care) EU-wide, including 2.1 million in care (ELA)–leading to social exclusion of workers, labor rights violations, fiscal

losses and uneven care quality. In some countries up to 50% of home care operates informally, causing “significant tax losses, poor working conditions, and labor shortages”. Without intervention, this harmful informality (amounting in fact to undeclared work) will deepen as Europe’s population ages (the 65+ cohort will expand by tens of millions by 2040), straining families, social security and care systems alike.

This strategic document–informed by a series of dialogues between EU Member State experts on live-in care, including a 2-day in person workshop and a two-round Delphi consultation with experts from multiple EU countries–proposes a three-pillar implementation strategy to support and formalize live-in caregiving, ensure fair mobility and conditions, and create a sustainable care model. It builds on top of previous proposals that identified policy options grounded in country-specific insightss. This strategic document aims to assess a feasible implementation of policies across various national contexts. The document does not reflect the official positions of the organizations involved in the project.

detail.abstract: Since returning to power in 2021, the Taliban has imposed one of the most repressive regimes for women in the modern era. This policy brief examines the far-reaching economic consequences of what has been described as gender apartheid. By excluding women and girls from education, employment, and public life, the Taliban has not only inflicted profound social harm but also dramatically reduced the country's economic potential. Drawing on available data, this analysis quantifies the cost of women's exclusion and shows how reversing these restrictions is essential not just for human rights, but for Afghanistan's long-term economic recovery.

affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Fossil-fuel abundance and CO2 emissions: Can financial development contribute to breaking the carbon curse?

publicationDetails.detailsText: ENEECO-D-25-03144

detail.abstract: Climate change has been linked to rising temperatures, extreme weather events, biodiversity loss, and sea-level rise. In this context, it is crucial to assess whether financial development can contribute to reducing carbon intensity, particularly in resource-rich countries. This paper explores the role of two structural characteristics, the degree of economic transformation and the presence of fossil-fuel subsidies, reflecting each country’s climate policy stance. A more advanced financial system may facilitate the reallocation of capital away from fossil fuel-intensive activities toward cleaner, service-oriented sectors, thereby reducing CO2 emissions per unit of GDP. We analyze the 45 highest CO2-emitting countries, which together accounted for over 90% of global emissions between 1990 and 2019. To estimate the relationship between financial development and carbon intensity, we employ a system Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) estimator. Our results suggest that financial development is associated with lower carbon intensity, but only in countries with a well-developed service sector and no fossil-fuel subsidies.

detail.abstract:
• Canadians and elected representatives wanting to know how their federal, provincial and territorial governments tax and spend, and how their capacity to deliver services is changing, face too many obstacles. As grades ranging from A+ to D- in this report card reveal, some governments provide useful and timely information, but too many present information that is opaque, late or both.

• In this year’s report card – which covers year-end financial statements for fiscal year 2023/24, and budgets and estimates for 2024/25 – Alberta topped the class with an A+. Quebec earned a B+; Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Saskatchewan, British Columbia, Yukon and Nunavut earned Bs; and Ontario earned a B-. Newfoundland and Labrador received a C. The federal government earned a D. At the bottom of the class, with D- grades, were Manitoba and the Northwest Territories.

• The fiscal transparency of Canada’s senior governments has improved over time, notably their adherence to Public Sector Accounting Standards (PSAS) in financial statements and more recently in budgets. But timeliness is a continuing problem and backsliding is a constant risk. Especially lately, the gaps between surpluses or deficits in budget projections and end-of-year results are disconcertingly large. Canadians need less backsliding and further progress to get better fiscal accountability from their governments.

detail.title: Stablecoin Performance in Cross-Border Payments: Evidence from a Digital Dollar Wallet

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author worked at Airtm from Jan 2022 to Dec 2023.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by the Future of Digital Currency Initiative at Stanford University.

detail.abstract: This paper presents empirical evidence on the performance of dollar-based stablecoins in crossborder payments, drawing on a five-year dataset of over 41 million transactions from Airtm—a global digital dollar wallet and payment platform. The analysis benchmarks Airtm’s transaction speed and cost against targets set by the G20 Roadmap for Enhancing Cross-Border Payments. The findings show that stablecoin payments significantly outperform traditional systems in speed, with more than 96% of transactions settling in under one hour, far exceeding G20 benchmarks. Cost outcomes are more varied: while 51% of Airtm transactions meet the 3% fee target and 36.7% meet the 1% fee target, fees remain higher for certain transaction categories, particularly P2P marketplace on- and off-ramps. Importantly, stablecoins enable new types of cross-border activity, such as micropayments under $2, which accounted for nearly half of enterprise disbursements. Taken together, the evidence highlights stablecoins’ potential to expand access to faster, lowercost, and more flexible cross-border payment systems, while also raising important considerations for regulation and market design. The paper concludes with policy recommendations on stablecoin usage including receiver access to stablecoins in payment flows, support for open network stablecoins, the impact of stablecoins to global labor markets and the importance of stablecoins for US currency competitiveness.

detail.abstract: This study presents a comprehensive analysis of various aspects of the rice processing industry in Bangladesh, such as rice cultivation, rice market, rice milling, competitiveness, future outlook, socio-economic condition, and profitability. Both primary and secondary data sources have been employed for this study. The preliminary data from 50 rice mills in five districts have been collected through the convenience sampling method. However, the study first provides a detailed discourse on rice cultivation in Bangladesh, which includes agroclimatic conditions, rice growing season and crop calendar, rice cultivars, factors affecting rice cultivation, and strategies to overcome problems associated with rice cultivation. Then, the study analyzes the rice market in Bangladesh, including rice production and consumption, growth, demand, import-export, and price trend. Next, the study focuses on rice milling in Bangladesh, which includes the type of rice mills, establishment and operational cost, production process, global supply chain, marketing channel, and related aspects. Moreover, competitive analysis is conducted using Porter's Five Forces Model, PESTEL analysis, and SWOT analysis. The study also predicts the industry's future, including opportunities and challenges, and provides a socio-economic profile of owners. Furthermore, the study summarizes the total cost, revenue, current asset, fixed asset, insurance, mortgage, and loan and discusses the problems and prospects the owners face in operating the business. The study reveals that the average total revenue for micro firms is Tk.172.04 million, for small firms is Tk.509.44 million, for medium firms, is Tk.968.53 million, and for large firms, Tk.1819.01 million. The benefit-cost ratio is 1.05, 1.11, 1.08, and 1.03 for micro, small, medium, and large firms, respectively. The average total benefit-cost ratio for the rice processing industry is 1.07. Finally, the study concludes by discussing some policy implications of the rice processing industry in Bangladesh.

title: Two-Stage Asymmetric Tullock Contests with Cost Shifters and Endogenous Continuation Decision

detail.title: Two-Stage Asymmetric Tullock Contests with Cost Shifters and Endogenous Continuation Decision
detail.abstract: This paper introduces a contest-theoretic simplified model of triathlon as a sequential two-stage game. In Stage 1 (post-swim), participants decide whether to continue or withdraw from the contest, thereby generating an endogenous participation decision. In Stage 2 (bike-run), competition is represented as a Tullock contest in which swim drafting acts as a multiplicative shifter of quadratic effort costs. Closed-form equilibrium strategies are derived in the two-player case, and existence, uniqueness, and comparative statics are shown in the asymmetric n-player case. The continuation decision yields athlete-specific cutoff rules in swim drafting intensity and induces subgame-perfect equilibria (SPEs) with endogenous participation sets. The analysis relates swim drafting benefits, exposure, and group size to heterogeneous effective cost parameters and equilibrium efforts.

title: The Deep Root of Economic Crises: The Physical Constraint of Time

detail.title: The Deep Root of Economic Crises: The Physical Constraint of Time
detail.abstract: This paper introduces the concept of the time constraint as a central framework for understanding the origins of economic crises. Unlike mainstream explanations that emphasize overproduction, insufficient demand, or monetary imbalance, the analysis highlights the finite nature of aggregate labor time and the time allocated to consumption activities as the ultimate limits on social wealth. By constructing a framework of the "four temporal dimensions of commodities" (production, price, utility, and consumption), the paper identifies two binding mechanisms: the purchasing power constraint and the consumption-time constraint. Crises arise when productivity grows faster than households' effective purchasing power and their capacity to allocate time to consumption. Historical evidence from the British crisis of 1825, the Great Depression of 1929, and the financial crisis of 2008 illustrates how different episodes reflect distinct forms of temporal mismatch, consistent with long-run analyses of financial instability (Kindleberger & Aliber, 2005). The discussion further evaluates Keynesian-style policy responses, arguing that while such measures may temporarily stabilize output and employment (Keynes, 1936), they often exacerbate the underlying structural imbalances of limited purchasing power and rising inequality. Consequently, economic crises should be understood not merely as cyclical market fluctuations but as systemic outcomes of imbalances between aggregate labor time and consumption-time capacity. The framework proposed here is intended to provide a foundation for further interdisciplinary research.

title: Thee Collaboration of Super Natural Intelligence (SNI), Natural Intelligence (SI), and Artificial Intelligence (AI) Towards the Attainment of Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)
affiliations: Mirracle Consultants and Mirracle Consultants

detail.title: Thee Collaboration of Super Natural Intelligence (SNI), Natural Intelligence (SI), and Artificial Intelligence (AI) Towards the Attainment of Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)
detail.abstract: The focus on the subject of intelligence has recently gained ground, particularly because of concerns regarding artficial intelligence (AI) replacing natural intelligence (NI). Developers of AI have different agendas, and have been encouraged to be ethical in their pursuits. In core, ethical AI development is aimed at ensuring the safety of humanity. Educational institutions are currently restructing their courses in an attempt not to produce obsolete graduates. However, in the realm of intelligence, there is one form of intelligence that is beyond scientific understanding, and this is supernatural intelligence (SI). Essentially, SI is the foundation of the other two forms of intelligence. Thus, a thorough understanding of the relationships among these forms of intelligence becomes non-negotiable, particularly in relation to the achievement of development goals. The 2015 transition from Millenium Development Goals (MDGs) to Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), signalled the need to further achieve certain key development goals. The current concerns surrounding ethical AI development could be addressed by linking AI development to specific SDGs. Consequently, the main objectives of this study were to 1) interrogate the connectedness of the three forms of intelligence, thereby mapping out a way for effective collaboration among these forms of intelligence; and to elaborate how AI can foster the achievement of SDGs. To achieve the above, a desktop literature review was used. From the comparisons conducted, it was found that supernatural intelligence is on top, followed by natural intelligence, and finally artficial intelligence. Furthermore, if properly aligned, these forms of intelligence have been found to have the capability to positively impact the societies through the speedy achievement of SDGs.

title: Biodiversity Loss and Firms' Financial Fragility
affiliations: Alma Mater Studiorum University of Bologna, Università degli studi di Modena e Reggio Emilia (UNIMORE), University College Dublin and

detail.title: Biodiversity Loss and Firms' Financial Fragility
detail.abstract: We assess the relation between biodiversity loss derived from a firm's activity and the firm's financial fragility. Using a global sample of publicly traded firms from 2018 to 2022, we show that biodiversity loss due to the firms' activities, primarily in a direct manner (through Scope 1 impacts), increases the firm's own default risk. Firms contributing to biodiversity-loss increase inventory as a buffer against ecosystem disruption and supply chain vulnerabilities, which increases funding needs and raises default risk. Firms' impact on biodiversity also translates into higher operating costs, which is evidence of physical risk exposure, and into higher equity price volatility and cost of debt. The impact, consistent with transition risk also playing an important role, is more substantial when investors' awareness increases in the post-COVID period and in countries with high extinction risk, and regulatory uncertainty amplifies the effect in countries lacking biodiversity and environmental protection policies. Beyond default risk, we find that biodiversity loss amplifies firms' financial fragility by strengthening the sensitivity of investments and cash holdings to internally generated cash flows, indicating tighter financial constraints.

detail.abstract: Persistent job vacancies in the United States represent a substantial unrealized component of gross domestic product (GDP). Using August 2025 Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey data and Current Employment Statistics earnings, this study estimates that unfilled positions equate to $453 billion in annual foregone labor income, translating to approximately $823 billion in potential GDP output. A novel technological intervention is proposed: an AI system that converts any job description into a deployable suite of task-aligned agents, prompts, and instructions for human integration. This approach reframes vacancies as capability gaps rather than solely labor supply shortages, offering a computational means of restoring lost output.

detail.abstract:
This work does not attempt to establish a new gravity theory, but instead employs a geometric–fluid model to reinterpret gravitational phenomena and make observationally testable predictions.


Key contributions include:

       1.    Axial infall as a geometric effect: We demonstrate that helical space flow naturally produces axial infall, offering a geometric explanation for gravitation.

       2.    Planetary dynamics: Calculations of Earth’s surface gravity g, the Sun’s gravitational field, and Mercury’s perihelion precession align with observed values.

       3.    Black hole predictions: We derive geometric scaling relations for black hole radii and masses, providing clear observational tests.

 

This study offers a complementary perspective to existing gravitational frameworks and suggests concrete comparisons with astronomical observations.

detail.abstract: In macroeconomics, forecasted data are often constructed as an aggregate over some time interval, such as monthly average prices or quarterly total output. We demonstrate that assessing the null of no directional accuracy requires computing the sign of change relative to the latest disaggregated observation rather than the latest aggregated observation. Changes are predictable by construction when assessed relative to the latest aggregated observation, resulting in inflated type I error and loss of power under the alternative. In contrast, assessing the change in the temporal aggregate relative to the latest disaggregated observation results in expected success ratios of 0.5, hypothesis tests with the intended type I error rate, and high power under the alternative.

detail.abstract: I develop a multi-agent LLM framework that processes Federal Reserve communications to construct narrative monetary policy surprises. By analyzing Beige Books and Minutes released before each FOMC meeting, the system generates conditional expectations that yield less noisy surprises than market-based measures. These surprises produce theoretically consistent impulse responses where contractionary shocks generate persistent disinflationary effects and enable profitable yield curve trading strategies that outperform alternatives. title: Between Autonomy and Spousal Backlash: Are Working Women Penalized in India?

detail.title: Between Autonomy and Spousal Backlash: Are Working Women Penalized in India?
detail.abstract: Although employment is often positioned as a pathway to women empowerment, empirical evidence on how social meanings attached to employment status shape intimate relations is conflicting. Leveraging nationally representative data from India, I explore whether women's employment status drives differential risks of spousal violence, comparing outcomes between employed and non-employed women. Estimates accounting for endogeneity show that employed women are penalized by spousal violence, with a 14.3 percentage point gap relative to nonemployed counterparts. This risk-enhancing effect of employment is pronounced across the socioeconomic spectrum and in rural India. Additionally, I examine mechanisms associated with bargaining and gender deviance neutralization theories and find that the observed marital abuse penalty is consistent with spousal backlash, which counteracted protective effects of women's autonomy. However, there is no evidence that women's beliefs justifying spousal abuse mediate the link between employment and violence. Collectively, our findings highlight the strong effect of social norms on intimate lives of Indian women, providing compelling evidence that attenuating these entrenched norms is crucial for their well-being.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the complex dynamics of inflation in India through a mixture of traditional econometric methods and advanced wavelet approaches. Using an Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) specification and wavelet coherence test with quarterly data between 2004 and 2024, we explore the complex interactions among inflation and its main drivers across various time-frequency spaces. The ARDL model confirms the major impact that oil has on inflation while also revealing a counterintuitive relationship between the output gap and inflation. The wavelet coherence analysis uncovers critical insights about the variation of this relationship over the time-frequency domain. We notice that there is a significant shift from short-term cycles to long-term cycles post-2016. This result suggests that inflation has become more structurally ingrained with time in the Indian Economy. Oil prices show the strongest and the most consistent relationship with inflation across all time horizons, while the exchange rate shows weak short-term relationships but strong long-term coherence.The 2008 Financial Crisis, the 2016 Demonetization, and the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic emerged as key inflection points that fundamentally altered cyclical patterns. By uncovering the time-varying character of economic relationships that may be ignored by traditional methods, this study adds to a more refined comprehension of inflation dynamics in emerging economies and offers useful insights for policymakers dealing with the challenges of price stability in an increasingly integrated global economy.

title: The Impact of Observing the Outcomes Obtained by Others: More Risk Taking, Or Less Sensitivity to Rare Events?

detail.title: The Impact of Observing the Outcomes Obtained by Others: More Risk Taking, Or Less Sensitivity to Rare Events?

keywords: Economics: Behavior and Behavioral Decision Making

detail.abstract: Previous research demonstrates that the tendency to imitate successful others can lead to counterproductive risk-taking. This research examines the boundaries of that effect across two preregistered experiments (N = 1,500; participants recruited via Prolific), in which individuals observed the outcomes of 20 investors who chose risky options and 20 who chose safe ones. Study 1 shows that observing others increases risk-taking when risky choices involve rare but highly unattractive outcomes ("rare disasters") yet leads to decreased risk-taking when risky choices offer rare but highly attractive outcomes ("rare treasures"). Study 2 examines the robustness of the finding that in rare treasure settings observing the performance of other investors reduces risk taking. It shows that this pattern emerges even when the performance of the most successful investor is highlighted, and even when the decision makers are asked to explicitly state which investor they wish to imitate. These findings suggest that observing others' outcomes reduces sensitivity to rare events and can be explained by assuming a two-stage process: first, a comparison of feasible action classes based on small samples, followed by a tendency to imitate the best performer within the chosen class. The results have direct implications for designing incentive systems when behavior is shaped by observational learning. For example, deterrence strategies are likely to be more effective when punishment is highly probable rather than severe but rare. In addition, the results help explain persistent under-diversification in lifelong financial decisions.

detail.abstract:
Plastic is an inescapable part of our lives. This dissertation is typed from a computer that is mainly made of plastic. The pen that is used to mark this dissertation will likely be made of plastic. In fact, plastic is just about everywhere. There are constant reminders in the news about what we are doing to our planet, our devastating impact on wildlife, the environment and other social costs. Yet, what is the economic cost of plastic pollution? Is it costing us more to pollute than abate? And what can we do to solve it?

detail.title: Disparities in Avoidable Mortality During the COVID-19 Pandemic Associated with State Partisan Orientation

detail.abstract:
Context: The politicization of the COVID-19 pandemic produced a sharp partisan divide in states' messaging and implementation of pandemic control policies, the public's willingness to change personal behaviors and be vaccinated, and COVID-19 cases and death rates. The goal of this analysis is to quantify the disparities in avoidable mortality associated with state-level partisan control, both before and after vaccines became available. 

Methods: Excess mortality rates were obtained from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. We identified five periods during which epidemiological patterns and interventions varied and grouped states into four categories reflecting different levels of partisan control of the governor's seat and the legislature. Avoidable mortality rates were calculated for each state by subtracting from excess mortality rates the average rate in the 20% of states with the lowest excess death rates in each period. 

Findings: More than half a million deaths could have been avoided during the COVID-19 pandemic had all states experienced the excess mortality rates of the best-performing quintile. The majority (320,162 deaths) occurred in states with Republican governors and legislatures, 25% greater than their share of the population. Almost 300,000 avoidable deaths occurred before vaccines were available, potentially reflecting earlier relaxation and weaker implementation of non-pharmaceutical interventions and related behaviors in Republican-controlled states. The disparity in avoidable death rates after vaccines became available was likely driven by sharp differences by state in vaccine uptake, especially in younger adults. 

Conclusions: Partisan choices made by state policymakers and the public are likely to have contributed to substantial mortality differentials during the pandemic. While there were benefits associated with less restrictive policies, partisan choices made by state policymakers and the public are likely to have contributed to large mortality disparities during the pandemic.

title: Endogenous Annual-Scale Dynamics in NASDAQ Volatility: A State-Space and Synchronization Reappraisal

detail.title: Endogenous Annual-Scale Dynamics in NASDAQ Volatility: A State-Space and Synchronization Reappraisal
detail.abstract: We analyze long-term periodicities in NASDAQ volatility using a unified framework that combines high-resolution spectral estimation, a state-space oscillator (SSO) model, exogenousdriver coherence tests, and phase-synchronization diagnostics. The cleaned daily dataset reveals three persistent annual-scale components at 372.4, 409.6, and 455.1 days. A fixed three-tone regression explains only R 2 = 0.062 of the standardized Hurst series, whereas the SSO-with time-varying amplitudes and phases-achieves R 2 = 0.464. Coherence with FOMC, quarterend, and tax-day calendars is uniformly weak (< 0.1), while phase locking between the 410-and 455-day components is strong and significant. These results demonstrate slow endogenous modulation between coupled macroeconomic cycles rather than a discrete structural regime shift.

title: When Rationality Fails: Economic Decision-Making Logic in an International Context

detail.title: When Rationality Fails: Economic Decision-Making Logic in an International Context
detail.abstract: When discussing decision-making, particularly economic decision-making, mainstream research typically confines its frame of analysis to the paradigms of 'absolute rationality' and 'bounded rationality'. This dualistic, formulaic mode of thinking extracts the decision-making process from its embedded social context, overlooking the structural characteristics of late capitalism and the interactive mechanisms between systems. Consequently, it reveals significant limitations and inadequacies in explaining decision-making behaviour within contemporary complex societies. Whilst economic practice has already exposed the distortions inherent in the 'absolute rationality' assumption, the decision-making behaviours of individuals and organisations in reality also reflect the intrinsic flaws of the so-called more academically robust 'bounded rationality' theory, this theory over-relies on the closed logic and abstract assumptions of economic models, failing to adequately incorporate the influence of social, cultural, and institutional variables. Consequently, it fosters an idealised, isolated conception of rationality. Therefore, this paper proposes that decision-making should not be assessed solely based on rationality, but rather viewed it as a dynamic product of the interaction between individual motivations and systemic incentives.Rationality is not a static or autonomous attribute, but a generative outcome shaped by context and constrained by structure. In other words, the degree of 'rationality' in decision-making is fundamentally a socioeconomic configuration jointly shaped by economic and social systems.

detail.abstract: In the Google Search antitrust litigation, the district court relied on a behavioral-economics model of consumer irrationality in finding that default placements amplify users’ inertia bias and inhibit migration away from Google search to alternative providers despite negligible switching costs.  This paper evaluates whether that proposition, and the underlying user-inertia assumption, withstands empirical scrutiny.  While the user-inertia model has been endorsed by regulators and a significant portion of antitrust scholarship, a broad review of evidence from general search, specialized search, answer-engine and search-adjacent markets shows that it has difficulty accounting for the diverse range of user conduct in the search ecosystem.  Users regularly multi-home across general search, specialized search, and answer-engine services and override defaults in search and other technology environments when they do not match user preferences. The user-inertia model also fails to account for Google’s inability to achieve adoption in specialized search markets, despite the use of default-like strategies, and Google’s currently lagging position in the answer engine market.  Given the divergence between the user-inertia model and user conduct in the search landscape, I present and apply an alternative model of adaptively rational user choice, where default effects vary depending on multiple factors that impact decision costs, including task complexity, learning costs, data portability, choice reversibility, and multi-homing capacities.  This model exhibits the best explanatory fit with variations in user conduct across search, search-adjacent, answer-engine, and other technology environments, rather than the prevailing model that assumes default settings uniformly lock in users and shield incumbent platforms from entry.  This model also reflects more accurately the diverse range of empirical findings on the status quo bias and default effects in the social science literature on which behavioral antitrust scholarship ultimately relies.

detail.title: Unveiling the Global Determinants and Effects of Bilingual Education Policies in Africa
detail.abstract: Despite the linguistic consensus that learning in one's mother tongue is better for learning, some African countries still use the colonial language as the official language of instruction in primary schools. This paper investigates the determinants and impacts of bilingual education reforms in Africa, which have replaced colonial languages with local languages as the medium of instruction since independence. Utilizing a unique dataset on linguistic policies, I find that a British colonial legacy and lower ethnolinguistic diversity increase the likelihood of implementing such reforms. An analysis of microdata from 18 countries covering almost 3 million of individuals reveals that these policies marginally enhanced schooling and learning outcomes, particularly for women and in countries prioritizing a large integration of local languages in education. The findings highlight the modest benefits of bilingual education and the challenges in its implementation, with implications for education policy in post-colonial settings.

title: Information Exchanges Involving AI Pricing Algorithms
affiliations: University of Chicago

detail.title: Information Exchanges Involving AI Pricing Algorithms
detail.abstract:
Pricing algorithms have long been used by individual firms to handle the nuances of market conditions. However, advances in machine learning and artificial intelligence have improved the power and accuracy of these models, making them increasingly vital components in a variety of industries. This paper focuses on shared pricing algorithms, typically offered as an external service.

Algorithms provided as a service to firms that may be competitors are not inherently anticompetitive or illegal. This service can improve pricing accuracy in industries with dynamic supply and demand, leading to more stable and efficient economic equilibriums. However, shared pricing algorithms can produce competitive threats and merit a fact-based inquiry. The central question is whether an algorithm replaces the pricing function at the firm level, or whether it operates to fix prices across a market. Key algorithmic features that establish an algorithm is operating at the market level are the known sharing of information across client firms, the supplying of prices directly to firms, and binding or pseudo-binding lock-in.

This paper shows how information sharing, price setting, and lock-in can individually raise the threat of competitive harm. A shared pricing algorithm with these features possesses the incentive and ability to foster a collusive outcome. Where information sharing occurs with the awareness and participation of client firms and deviation from the algorithm’s prices is made cumbersome by lock-in, a shared pricing algorithm fixes prices in violation of Section 1 of the Sherman Act.

To illustrate the competitive harm that can result from shared pricing algorithms, this paper focuses on the ongoing public and private antitrust cases against RealPage, a pricing algorithm operating in multi-family real estate. RealPage’s utilization of known information sharing across clients, price setting, and pseudo-binding lock-in create a powerful nexus that enables a collusive outcome in violation of antitrust law.

detail.title: The Invisible Elbow: Can Green Nudges Correct Market Failures without Coercion?
detail.abstract: The idea of green nudges-subtle behavioral economics-based interventions that foster environmentally friendly choices without limiting consumer freedom-is explored in this study. The research examines how correcting market failures in environmental issues, such pollution, may be achieved by nudges including default settings, social norms, and timing nudges. Internalizing bad environmental externalities and data failures. Through empirical case studies including electricity-saving behavior and green energy defaults in Germany, the efficacy of green nudges like energy-saving prompts and renewable energy defaults is considered. Challenges still exist, therefore, in guaranteeing transparency, justice, and ongoing efficiency. Green nudges derive from behavioral sciences, particularly behavioural economics, which recognise that consumers do not always behave rationally due to biases, emotions, lack of perfect knowledge, trends, advertising, peer pressure, etc. From this, "green nudges" are defined as interventions that subtly encourage environmentally friendly decisions, but are non-restrictive of consumer freedom and do not use regulatory coercion. They include types such as default options, social norms, salience nudges, and timing nudges.

detail.abstract: Interviews allow employers to learn about workers, but do they also enable workers to learn about firms? Studying 500,000 interview reports from Glassdoor, we find candidates for high-paying jobs are more likely to reject a job offer if they believe the interview was easy. Easy interviews appear to convey poor "fit" as those who accept offers after easy interviews are two-fifths of a standard deviation less satisfied with their jobs and 10 percent less likely to remain with their employer for at least one year. Analysis of interview narratives using large language models reveals difficult interviews signal colleague ability whereas easy interviews convey a nonselective process. In a small-scale randomized field experiment, an exogenous increase in difficulty elevated perceived difficulty and boosted applicant engagement with the vacancy. Interviews offer workers a preview of match quality, highlighting a channel through which labor markets may become less efficient if firms automate hiring with AI.

detail.abstract: This study addresses the challenge of forecasting maize yield in southeastern Quebec by comparing weekly Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) and PlanetScope satellite imagery throughout the cropping season and across diverse growing conditions. Using five nitrogen treatments over three years with two sowing windows each year to generate variability within the dataset, eleven vegetation indices were evaluated to identify the best performing ones and the optimal forecasting window. Indices were interpolated using curve fitting to enable evaluation at any stage of the growing season. Cross-validation simulated real-world application by excluding entire sowing events during model testing. Using a linear regression approach, results demonstrate that indices combining green and near-infrared bands (Green Normalized Difference Vegetation Index [GNDVI] and Chlorophyll Index Green [Cig]) exhibit superior forecasting potential compared to red-near-infrared (like NDVI) and RGB-based indices (like NGRDI). The optimal forecast window occurs during early grain filling (R2-R3 stages, around 2300 Crop Heat Units [CHU]), achieving Root Mean Square Coefficient of Variation (RMSCV) values of 12.51% for UAVs and 15.28% for PlanetScope. While PlanetScope maximum performance approached UAV capabilities, results showed a 50-day reduction in the effective forecasting period (RMSCV < 20%). For PlanetScope, adding multiple indices marginally improved precision, slightly reduced forecasting window and reduced model transferability. The analysis revealed weak correlations between indices and yield during early vegetative and senescence phases, indicating limited potential for enabling timely in-season management interventions. This study established UAV-based models as a reference point for assessing the limitations of satellite-derived forecasts.

Portuguese Abstract: Os direitos das minorias sexuais e de género começaram a ser reivindicados em finais da década de 60 e inícios da década de 70 do século passado. Apesar de ter mais de meio-século de vida, a distinção entre sexo e género é ainda considerada um tema de vanguarda e objeto de sonora politização e hiperbolização ideológica . Desde logo, os temas do sexo e do género não são imunes a distintas valorações culturais, morais e religiosas . Mas não só isso: desvenda-se uma espécie de guerra dogmático-cultural e identitária entre conservadores e progressistas, com duras acusações mútuas de ‘ultraconservadorismo’, ‘ideologia patriarcal’, ‘masculinidade tóxica’ ou ‘conservadorismo antifeminista’, de um lado, e de ‘ativismo radical’, ‘colonização ideológica’, ‘marxismo cultural’ ou ‘wokismo identitário’, de outro lado . 
 Num mundo complexo, assiste-se a uma profunda divisão entre os que louvam, por razões de justiça social e de acolhimento da diversidade e do pluralismo, a maior visibilidade cívica e política de grupos tradicionalmente marginalizados, e os que alertam para as ameaças à liberdade de expressão e à liberdade académica, em particular, aos dilemas da ‘cultura de cancelamento’, da autocensura alienante, da tendência de confirmação (confirmation bias), e da pressão do ‘politicamente correto’ . 
 Como alicerçar pontes em águas tão movediças? Como encontrar um caminho em labirintos mundividenciais? Neste contexto tão atribulado, um debate esclarecido sobre os temas do sexo e do género não pode dispensar as aprendizagens da evolução científica, em especial da genética, da biologia, da medicina, das neurociências, da psicologia, da sociologia, da antropologia, entre outras. Em acréscimo, importa salientar o potencial conciliador da serena moderação, num delicado equilíbrio entre, por um lado, a rejeição de superioridades morais apriorísticas e a concomitante recusa da substituição da educação pela doutrinação ideológica e, por outro lado, o respeito pela diversidade e pela igual dignidade de todos os seres humanos. 

English Abstract: Claims to sexual and gender minority rights began to emerge in the late 1960s and early 1970s. Despite over half a century of development, the distinction between sex and gender remains both a frontier topic and a focus of intense politicisation and ideological exaggeration. These issues are shaped not only by varied cultural, moral, and religious evaluations, but also by a dogmatic, cultural, and identity-based struggle between conservatives and progressives. Each side directs accusations of “ultraconservatism,” “patriarchal ideology,” “toxic masculinity,” or “antifeminist conservatism” on one hand, and “radical activism,” “ideological colonisation,” “cultural Marxism,” or “identity wokism” on the other. 
In an increasingly complex world, a profound divide persists between those who, in the name of social justice and pluralism, applaud the civic and political visibility of traditionally marginalised groups, and those who warn of threats to freedom of expression and academic freedom, particularly regarding “cancel culture,” alienating self-censorship, confirmation bias, and the constraints of political correctness.
How may bridges be built across such turbulent waters? How might one find a path through such labyrinthine worldviews? In this fraught context, any informed debate on sex and gender must engage with the advances of the sciences—genetics, biology, medicine, neuroscience, psychology, sociology, and anthropology. Moreover, balanced moderation remains vital: a careful equilibrium between rejecting moral superiority and ideological indoctrination, and affirming respect for diversity and the equal dignity of all human beings.

detail.abstract: Agriculture is an economic activity that depends on exogenous factors such as climate. Thus, climatic conditions can impact productivity and production, and therefore, prices. This paper aims to study the influence of climatic shocks (excessive or insufficient rainfall) on the prices of grains (beans, corn, and rice) in Nicaragua, using a unique set of climatic data at the municipal level. Using structural vector autoregressive models with exogenous variables (SVAR-X), it is found that basic prices in the country react to weather conditions heterogeneously, i.e., depending on the planting phase. Increases in corn prices are evident due to lack of rainfall during the "primera" planting phase. Meanwhile, excess rainfall pushes up bean prices during the "postrera" planting phase, but is associated with downward pressure on rice prices during the "primera" planting phase. Thus, a combined weather shock could explain between 0.7 and 0.8 percentage points of inflation in the country.

title: An Overlooked Force in Dynamic Pricing: How Strategic Early Disposals Come into Play

detail.title: An Overlooked Force in Dynamic Pricing: How Strategic Early Disposals Come into Play
detail.abstract: Salvage value changes over time due to market dynamics or the time value of money. Yet, most existing dynamic pricing models assume a constant salvage value over time, which is amenable to the long-standing simplification of normalizing it to zero, thereby overlooking its strategic impact. When the constant salvage value assumption no longer holds, early disposal emerges endogenously as a vital part of the optimal policy of the resulting stochastic control problem. To accommodate the reshaped optimal strategy, which integrates dynamic pricing with sequential disposals, we must resort to a system of quasi-variational inequalities (QVI) to define the value function of the problem, as opposed to the standard Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation used in the dynamic pricing literature. Through a rigorous analysis of the QVI, we identify disposal regions in both deterministic and stochastic salvage-value settings, providing a comprehensive foundation for understanding when and why early disposal becomes optimal. In particular, we show that disposal regions exhibit a nested structure that aligns with the sequential nature of inventory depletion. Beyond methodological contributions, our findings reveal practically relevant conditions under which early disposal alleviates inventory pressure and improves expected revenue, particularly in environments with significant discounting or stochastic salvage values.

detail.abstract: This paper re-examines the response of parental labor supply to the pandemic-era suspension of in-person instruction. The effect of school closures is undetectable after controlling comprehensively for unobserved heterogeneity. Even excluding such controls, a shift from fully virtual to in-person implies an increase in weekly hours worked of just 2 to 2.5. These estimates are used to inform a simple model of the household in which access to telework and nonparental care mitigate the labor supply impact of school closures. Time use data suggest telework and nonparental care indeed helped some parents balance work and childcare during the pandemic.
